snippet.title: Starhawk Longplay (Arcade Version)
snippet.description:
- Starhawk Longplay (Arcade Version) -

Starhawk is a first-person vector shooter designed and programmed by Tim Skelly and released by Cinematronics in 1979. Arriving two years after the original Star Wars film, it makes no great effort to disguise its inspiration: a long, receding space trench, enemy craft approaching from the distance and a viewpoint that places the player in the middle of a science-fiction dogfight. It was an impressive spectacle for its time, even without an official connection to George Lucas's universe.

Rather than steering a visible spacecraft, you control a gunsight, tracking targets as they appear against the rapidly moving landscape. Fighters, bombers, missiles and other objects emerge at different distances and speeds, and every successful hit adds to your score. The shooting itself is immediate, but judging where a small enemy will be by the time you line up a shot takes more practice than the simple screen might suggest.

One particularly unusual feature of the original cabinet is its three aiming-speed buttons. Alongside the joystick and firing control, they let you select slow, medium or fast movement for the gunsight. Slow movement helps with precision, while faster settings are useful when targets suddenly appear far from your current position. Switching between them is an important part of keeping up with the action; moving the sight at one speed all the time is rarely the best approach.

There is also a nasty surprise in the form of a command ship, sometimes called the Killer Ship. It makes an appearance amid the ordinary targets and can attack your score if you fail to deal with it quickly. Seeing hard-earned points disappear is a wonderfully cruel incentive to stop concentrating on the easy targets and take care of the more dangerous visitor.

The scoring system rewards different enemies according to their value, but the real opponent is the clock. The initial game is brief, with extra time awarded as your score crosses certain milestones. That changes the way you approach a run. A few accurate shots are not merely a way of climbing the scoreboard; they may also buy you the seconds needed to keep playing. There is no conventional sequence of stages to finish, just a continual fight to extend the session.

The black-and-white vector display is the main attraction. The trench seems to stream toward you in perspective, while enemy outlines grow and shift as they approach. It looks sparse beside later arcade games, yet the sense of depth was striking in 1979. The crisp geometry gives the action a look that ordinary sprite graphics would not have reproduced in quite the same way, and the sharp electronic shooting and explosion sounds suit it surprisingly well.

Of course, the illusion has limitations. The scenery changes little, the enemy patterns become familiar, and the activity is ultimately confined to moving a sight around a fairly uncluttered screen. Once the novelty of the perspective wears off, the game has to stand on the satisfaction of aiming and scoring alone. Whether that is enough depends on how much you enjoy the relentless, stripped-down design of the earliest arcade shooters.

I rather like the directness of it. There are no complicated rules to learn, no lengthy interruptions and nothing to distract from the immediate problem of finding and hitting the next target. The best moments come when several enemies enter the picture almost together and a quick adjustment of the aiming speed lets you catch them before they disappear. Missing an easy shot, meanwhile, is instantly annoying because you know exactly what went wrong.

Starhawk is not as varied or as enduring as some of the vector classics that followed, but it belongs to an intriguing moment when arcade designers were still discovering what three-dimensional movement could look like on a screen. The Star Wars influence is obvious, yet the timed scoring and variable-speed gunsight give it an identity of its own. It is a modest game today, certainly, but an enjoyable little piece of arcade history that still makes a good case for the excitement of glowing lines and a moving target.
